extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors and self-represented patent applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, beginner-oriented guidance for inventors who are drafting and filing their own patent claims (including use of provisional applications as disclosure). Focuses on how to write independent and dependent claims, antecedent basis, and describing component structure and connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a broad claim that defines your invention in broad terms
rubrics_metrics.description: First, include a claim that defines your invention in broad terms, leaving out any and all unnecessary options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad claims should omit unnecessary options so they capture the generic invention. The author recommends creating at least one broad/generic claim at the initial filing stage to 'bookend' the invention with a generic version. It's acceptable if the claim isn't in perfect Patent Office format at first — scope matters more initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a highly specific claim listing every option
rubrics_metrics.description: Include another claim that defines your invention with as much specificity and with every option you can think of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write dependent/narrow claims that add every possible optional feature or configuration you can imagine so you have specific fallbacks. Example: start with a generic peanut butter-and-jelly sandwich claim, then add a dependent claim listing bacon, lettuce, tomato and fluff. Having both broad and narrow claims 'bookends' the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start claims with 'A {title} comprising:' and list parts and connections
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting a claim you want to start with something like this: '1. A {insert title} comprising: {list the parts one by one} {then explain how each are connected}.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives a simple template and examples (peanut butter & jelly sandwich; shovel). Use 'comprising' and enumerate elements, then explain how elements are connected/interact. Don't worry about perfect Patent Office formatting at the drafting stage — focus on capturing parts and their relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe how components are structured and interact (must be complete and distinguish over prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a claim it is important to describe how the various components are structured and how the various components interact and connect. It is necessary to describe the invention so that it is complete, so that it works, but also so that it is different than what is known in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should make clear 'what makes your invention different' from prior art. Describe structure, interconnections, and operation sufficiently to define the invention and to enable understanding of distinctions from known devices or methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide proper antecedent basis (introduce elements with 'a/an' then refer with 'said'/'the')
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce elements with either 'a' or 'an' and then when you subsequently refer to the element refer to it by either 'said' or 'the,' hence introducing 'a shovel head' and then later referring to 'said shovel head.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal reference points to make it easier to describe how to connect elements. Avoid referring to an element as 'said X' before it has been introduced; doing so signals an improper antecedent basis and causes problems (e.g., mentioning 'said neck' when 'neck' wasn't previously introduced). If you need to reference sub-parts later, introduce them in the earlier claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dependent claims to narrow and add specific features
rubrics_metrics.description: In dependent claims you build on a claim earlier to narrow the description to make it more specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims should explicitly reference and add limitations to earlier claims (examples: adding 'a grip disposed around said second end' or specifying the grip material). Use dependent claims to create layers of fallback positions narrowing feature sets and specifying materials, attachments, and configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When adding specific connectors or attachments, introduce the referenced sub-elements first
rubrics_metrics.description: If you add a claim that depends on some sub-element (e.g., a neck) used to explain how a screw connects parts, you must first have introduced that sub-element in an earlier claim or modify the independent claim to introduce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to claim 'a screw through said neck' you should either have introduced 'a neck' in claim 1 (e.g., 'a shovel head, which is made up of a neck leading up into a blade') or modify the independent claim so that the sub-element has antecedent basis. Otherwise an examiner will flag improper antecedent basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: At the initial filing stage, include claims with appropriate scope even if not in perfect PTO format
rubrics_metrics.description: At the initial filing stage what matters most is that claims are present and they have appropriate scope, with some being broad and some being narrow and quite specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's more important to capture scope and alternatives than to have perfect formal language. Draft broad and narrow claims to 'bookend' the invention. Later you can refine to PTO-required formats, but failing to capture scope early can harm rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional patent applications: focus on broadest disclosure; claims are not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional patent applications, however, do not need claims and can and should focus on providing the broadest disclosure possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conscientious inventor can create a pretty good disclosure using a provisional, and then use that disclosure as the basis for later drafted claims. The author notes The Invent & Patent System™ helps create provisionals but does not try to create claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative drafting: start writing, add elements as needed, and check antecedent introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps the best way to go about writing claims is to just start writing, then as you need to add elements to the invention to define ever more specific versions check to see if the pieces and parts being added have been introduced properly and result in a description of the version that is complete and describes what you have pictured in your mind’s eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims iteratively: begin with basic independent claim(s), then add dependent claims and modify independent claims as needed to introduce sub-elements. Continuously check for completeness, antecedent basis, and whether the description conveys the intended embodiment(s). Recognize that drafting claims is difficult and that professional assistance improves outcomes.
